concepts.name: Algorithm
concepts.statement: An algorithm is an explicit, precise, unambiguous, mechanically executable sequence of elementary instructions, usually intended to accomplish a specific purpose.

concepts.name: Lattice multiplication
concepts.statement: Multiplying an m-digit number by an n-digit number by summing the partial products X[i] · Y[j] · 10^(i+j), in whatever order and with whatever handling of the carries, takes O(mn) time, dominated by the single-digit multiplications.

concepts.name: Peasant multiplication
concepts.statement: x · y can be computed with only parity tests, addition, doubling (duplation) and halving (mediation): halve x and double y, adding y to the product whenever x is odd; this takes O(log x) such steps and O(mn) time for an m-digit and an n-digit number.

concepts.name: Huntington–Hill apportionment
concepts.statement: Huntington–Hill gives each state one representative, then each next seat to the state of highest priority P/√(r(r+1)), held in a priority queue used only through NewPriorityQueue, Insert and ExtractMax; the output, and so its correctness, does not depend on how the queue is implemented.

concepts.name: Underspecified algorithm
concepts.statement: Martin’s “how to become a millionaire and never pay taxes” is not an algorithm, because its first step, get a million dollars, is not an elementary, unambiguous instruction; it is a perfectly good reduction.

concepts.name: Describing an algorithm
concepts.statement: A complete description of an algorithm gives what (a precise specification of the problem), how (the algorithm itself, loops written as loops and recursion as recursion), why (a proof that it solves the problem) and how fast (an analysis of its running time).

concepts.name: The need for efficiency
concepts.statement: Scanning every item does not scale: 10^6 searches over 10^6 items is 10^12 inspections, about 1000 seconds at 10^9 operations a second, so a data structure must be organised so that most operations inspect few items.

concepts.name: Interface and implementation
concepts.statement: An interface, or abstract data type, names the operations a data structure supports and what they mean; an implementation gives its internal representation and the algorithms for the operations. One interface can have many implementations.

concepts.name: Logarithms
concepts.statement: log_b k is the unique x with b^x = k; log with no base means log₂, and ln k is log_e k, the natural logarithm, with e ≈ 2.71828. log_b k is roughly the number of times k must be divided by b before the result is at most 1. A logarithm changes base as log_b k = log_a k / log_a b, so ln k = (ln 2)(log k).

concepts.name: Factorials and Stirling’s approximation
concepts.statement: n! = 1·2·…·n counts the orderings of n distinct elements, and 0! = 1. Stirling’s Approximation gives n! = √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ e^α(n) with 1/(12n + 1) < α(n) < 1/(12n), and so ln(n!) = n ln n − n + ½ ln(2πn) + α(n). The binomial coefficient n!/(k!(n − k)!) counts the k-element subsets of an n-element set.

forms.condition: for an integer k in {0, …, n}

concepts.name: Harmonic numbers
concepts.statement: The k-th harmonic number is H_k = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/k. It has no simple closed form, but ln k < H_k ≤ ln k + 1 for k ≥ 1, because H_k is the area of k unit-width rectangles that lie over the curve 1/x from 1, or, after the first, under it.

concepts.name: The w-bit word-RAM model
concepts.statement: Memory is cells, each holding a w-bit word; arithmetic, comparisons and bitwise operations on words take constant time, any cell is read or written in constant time, allocating a block of k words takes O(k) time, and the only assumption about the word size is w ≥ log n. Space is measured in words.

concepts.name: Analysing running time and space
concepts.statement: Measure an algorithm’s running time by counting how often it executes an instruction or reaches a milestone, as a function of its input: nested loops give nested sums, a recursive algorithm a recurrence, and the count may depend on how an underlying data structure is implemented; space and other resources are counted the same way.

concepts.name: Worst-case, amortized and expected running times
concepts.statement: A worst-case running time f(n) means no single operation ever takes longer than f(n); an amortized running time f(n) means any sequence of m operations takes at most m f(n); an expected running time f(n) means the running time is a random variable, over the data structure’s own random choices, whose expected value is at most f(n).

concepts.name: Amortized analysis
concepts.statement: Amortized analysis bounds the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, spreading the cost of occasional expensive operations (a resize) over the cheap ones; it involves no probability.

concepts.name: Aggregate analysis and the accounting method
concepts.statement: Bound the total cost of a sequence of operations by summing it and averaging it over the operations (aggregate analysis), or by charging each operation a fixed amortized cost whose surplus is stored as credit to pay for later expensive operations (the accounting method).

concepts.name: Potential method
concepts.statement: Define a potential Φ on the states of a data structure with Φ(S) ≥ Φ(S₀) for every reachable state; an operation’s amortized cost is its actual cost plus the change in Φ, and the total amortized cost of any sequence bounds its total actual cost.

concepts.name: Factorials, permutations and combinations
concepts.statement: If a whole can be divided into k parts with n_i choices for the i-th part, there are n₁ × n₂ × … × n_k ways of doing the whole; so there are n! orderings of n items, n!/(n − k)! ordered selections of k of them, and (n choose k) = n!/((n − k)! k!) unordered ones.

concepts.name: Basic probability
concepts.statement: The outcomes form the sample space Ω and an event is a subset of it; a probability measure Pr gives each event a number in [0, 1] with Pr(Ω) = 1, Pr(A) ≥ 0 and Pr(A ∪ B) = Pr(A) + Pr(B) − Pr(A ∩ B). When all N outcomes are equally likely, Pr(A) = |A|/N.

concepts.name: Conditional probability and independence
concepts.statement: Pr(A|K) = Pr(A ∩ K)/Pr(K) is the probability of A once K is known to have occurred; A and B are independent when Pr(A|B) = Pr(A), so that knowing one tells nothing about the other.

concepts.name: Random variable
concepts.statement: A random variable R on a probability space is a total function whose domain is the sample space, usually real-valued: every outcome determines its value, and an assertion about its value, such as [C = 2], is an event.

concepts.name: Expected value and linearity of expectation
concepts.statement: The expected value of a discrete random variable is E[X] = Σ_x x·Pr{X = x}; for any random variables, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] and E[Σ X_i] = Σ E[X_i], so a complicated random variable can be broken into a sum of simpler ones.

concepts.name: Indicator random variables
concepts.statement: Write a count as a sum of indicator variables I_i, each 1 if its event happens and 0 otherwise; then E[Σ I_i] = Σ Pr{I_i = 1}, as for the k/2 expected heads in k fair tosses.

concepts.name: Expected tosses until the first head
concepts.statement: If T is the number of times a fair coin is tossed up to and including the first time it comes up heads, then E[T] = 2.

concepts.name: Big-O notation
concepts.statement: For a function f(n), O(f(n)) is the set of functions g(n) for which there exist c > 0 and n₀ such that g(n) ≤ c·f(n) for all n ≥ n₀: an upper bound on growth, with constant factors and small n set aside.

forms.latex: O(f(n)) = \{\, g(n) : \text{there exists } c > 0 \text{ and } n_0 \text{ such that } g(n) \le c\cdot f(n) \text{ for all } n \ge n_0 \,\}

concepts.name: Big-Omega and Big-Theta
concepts.statement: T(n) is in Ω(g(n)) when there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that T(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n > n₀, a lower bound; it is Θ(h(n)) when it is in both O(h(n)) and Ω(h(n)); and the limit of f(n)/g(n) as n grows (∞, 0 or a constant other than zero) puts f(n) in Ω(g(n)), O(g(n)) or Θ(g(n)).

forms.latex: \mathbf{T}(n) \in \Omega(g(n)) \text{ if there exist } c > 0 \text{ and } n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } \mathbf{T}(n) \geq c\, g(n) \text{ for all } n > n_0
f(n) = \Theta(h(n)) \text{ if } f(n) \in O(h(n)) \text{ and } f(n) \in \Omega(h(n))

concepts.name: Analysis with multiple parameters
concepts.statement: When an algorithm’s cost depends on several parameters, the analysis keeps each one for the steps that depend on it (Θ(P + C log C) for P pixels and C colours) rather than folding them into one input size.

concepts.name: Prefix sums
concepts.statement: The prefix sums of a sequence a₁, …, aₙ (with a₀ = 0) are S_i = a₁ + ⋯ + a_i, computed one after another by S₀ = 0, S_i = S_{i−1} + a_i; after this O(n) preprocessing the sum of any range [l, r] is S_r − S_{l−1}, an O(1) query.

concepts.name: Two-dimensional prefix sums
concepts.statement: S_{i,j} = A_{i,j} + S_{i−1,j} + S_{i,j−1} − S_{i−1,j−1} fills the table of two-dimensional prefix sums in one pass, the subtraction removing the overlap the two sums both count (inclusion–exclusion); the sum of a submatrix is then four lookups, S_{i₂,j₂} − S_{i₁−1,j₂} − S_{i₂,j₁−1} + S_{i₁−1,j₁−1}. In k dimensions, summing along one dimension at a time costs O(kN), where inclusion–exclusion costs O(2^k N).

forms.condition: the sum of the submatrix with corners (i₁, j₁) and (i₂, j₂)

concepts.name: Difference arrays
concepts.statement: The difference sequence D_i = a_i − a_{i−1} (a₀ = 0) is the inverse of the prefix sum: adding v to every a_i with l ≤ i ≤ r becomes D_l ← D_l + v and D_{r+1} ← D_{r+1} − v, O(1) per update, and one O(n) prefix-sum pass after all the updates recovers the array.

forms.latex: D_{l} \gets D_{l} + v,~ D_{r+1}\gets D_{r+1} - v
forms.condition: to add v to every a_i in [l, r]

concepts.name: Two-dimensional difference arrays
concepts.statement: Adding v to every entry of the submatrix with corners (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) becomes four updates of the two-dimensional difference array, +v at (x₁, y₁) and (x₂ + 1, y₂ + 1) and −v at (x₁, y₂ + 1) and (x₂ + 1, y₁); one two-dimensional prefix-sum pass afterwards recovers the array. In k dimensions an update touches 2^k entries.

concepts.name: Floyd’s cycle detection (tortoise and hare)
concepts.statement: Start two pointers at the head, slow moving one node at a time and fast two; if they ever point to the same node the list has a cycle, and if fast reaches null it has none. Fast’s lead grows by one node a step, so once slow has moved a multiple kL ≥ a of the cycle’s length L, both are in the cycle, kL apart, and meet.

concepts.name: Finding where the cycle starts
concepts.statement: Once slow and fast meet, reset slow to the head and move both one node at a time; they meet at the node where the cycle starts.

concepts.name: Why the reset finds the cycle start
concepts.statement: With a the steps from the head to the cycle’s start C, b from C to the meeting point G, L the cycle’s length and x, y the laps of slow and fast, a + yL + b = 2(a + xL + b) gives a = (y − 2x)L − b: a steps from G is whole laps less b, which ends on C, as a steps from the head does.

concepts.name: Array
concepts.statement: An array is a collection of elements of one memory size, each identified by an index (or a tuple of indices), stored so that each element’s address is computed from its index by a formula: B + c·i in one dimension, B + c·i + d·j in two. Store and select take constant time, and the array takes O(n) space.

forms.latex: \text{address} = B + c_1 i_1 + c_2 i_2 + \dots + c_k i_k

concepts.name: Indexing by pointer arithmetic
concepts.statement: In C, a[i] is defined as *(a + i): an array’s name evaluates to a pointer to its first element, and adding i to a pointer moves it i elements on, i times the element’s size in bytes.

concepts.name: List interface
concepts.statement: A List represents a sequence x₀, …, x_{n−1} with size(), get(i), set(i, x), add(i, x), which shifts x_i, …, x_{n−1} one place right, and remove(i), which shifts the later values one place left. These subsume the Deque: addFirst(x) is add(0, x) and removeLast() is remove(size() − 1).

concepts.name: Dummy (sentinel) node
concepts.statement: A DLList keeps a dummy node that holds no data and stands after the last node and before the first, so the nodes form a cycle, every node has a next and a prev, and adding or removing needs no special case for an empty list or for either end.

concepts.name: Doubly linked list
concepts.statement: A linked list whose nodes point both to the node that follows them and to the node that precedes them; with a dummy node it reaches the ith node from the nearer end in O(1 + min{i, n − i}) time, and adds or removes a node it holds a reference to in constant time.

concepts.name: Dynamic array (vector)
concepts.statement: A list kept in a backing array a that is usually larger than it needs to be: n counts the elements, stored in a[0], …, a[n−1], and length(a) ≥ n at all times; when the array is full a larger one is allocated and the elements are copied into it.

concepts.name: Growing and shrinking the backing array
concepts.statement: resize() allocates an array b of size 2n, copies the n elements of a into its first n positions and makes b the new a, in O(n) time; add(i, x) calls it when a is full and remove(i) when length(a) ≥ 3n.

concepts.name: Cost of dynamic-array operations
concepts.statement: Ignoring resizing, get(i) and set(i, x) take O(1) time and add(i, x) and remove(i) take O(1 + n − i); from an empty ArrayStack, any m calls to add(i, x) and remove(i) spend O(m) time in all calls to resize(), so push and pop at the end run in O(1) amortized time.

concepts.name: Block copying with memcpy/arraycopy
concepts.statement: Shifting and copying with a platform's block-move functions (memcpy and memmove in C, std::copy in C++, System.arraycopy in Java) in place of for loops leaves the asymptotic running times unchanged but can be several times faster; ODS measured a factor between 2 and 3.

concepts.name: Implement a vector
concepts.statement: Build a resizable array: fields a and n, size, get, set, add(i, x) and remove(i) that shift the elements after i, and a resize that doubles the array when it is full and shrinks it when it is two-thirds empty; ODS's ArrayStack is such a class.

concepts.name: Singly linked list
concepts.statement: A linked list is a sequence of nodes whose order is not given by their place in memory: each node holds its data and a link (the next pointer) to the next node; the head is the first node, the last node links to a terminator, and a singly linked list’s nodes hold a value field and a next field.

concepts.name: Pointer to pointer
concepts.statement: Pass a function the address of a pointer (double indirection, LinkedList **), so that it can change where the caller’s pointer points: a list insert then updates the caller’s head correctly, with no special case for inserting at the front.

concepts.name: Implement a linked list
concepts.statement: Change a singly linked list in place: traverse by following next links from firstNode; insert or remove after a given node by re-aiming its link, in constant time; insert or remove at the beginning by updating firstNode; inserting before a node, or appending without a reference to the tail, needs a traversal (O(n)); a dummy first node removes the special cases.

concepts.name: Linked lists versus arrays
concepts.statement: A linked list inserts or deletes in constant time at a node already in hand (O(n) to find it) and grows without reallocation, but allows only sequential access, uses extra storage for links and has poorer locality of reference; a dynamic array gives constant-time random access and faster sequential access but moves elements to insert or delete in the middle.

concepts.name: Two pointers
concepts.statement: Two pointers point at positions of a sequence or a linked list (or at nodes of a tree or graph) and move in the same direction or toward each other to maintain or count information; on a sorted sequence, one at each end closes in on a pair with a given sum, each step moving the pointer whose element cannot be part of it.

concepts.name: 3SUM in quadratic time
concepts.statement: After sorting, 3SUM (do three of n numbers sum to zero?) is solved in worst-case O(n²) time without hashing: for each a = S[i], two pointers start = i + 1 and end = n − 1 move inward, end down when a + b + c > 0 and start up when it is < 0.

concepts.name: Merging two sorted lists
concepts.statement: Two sorted lists, linked lists or arrays, merge into one in linear time by repeatedly appending the smaller of their two heads (the head of A on a tie) and dropping it from its list, then appending what remains of the other.

concepts.name: Fixed-size sliding window
concepts.statement: A mean over the last k data points is updated as the window moves by adding the value that comes in and subtracting the one that drops out, SMA_next = SMA_prev + (p_{n+1} − p_{n−k+1})/k: three arithmetic steps, not a new sum of k values.

concepts.name: Variable-size sliding window
concepts.statement: Two pointers l and r bound a window over which a quantity that changes monotonically and is cheap to update (a sum of positive numbers, a product of positive integers) is kept: r moves right one element at a time and l moves right while the window breaks the condition, so for each r, l is the leftmost point the window can reach and the valid windows ending at r number r − l + 1.

concepts.name: Queue
concepts.statement: A Queue is a collection with add(x), which adds the value x, and remove(), which removes and returns the next value; its queueing discipline decides which value comes next, and a FIFO (first-in-first-out) Queue removes values in the order they were added. add(x) and remove() on a FIFO Queue are often called enqueue(x) and dequeue().

concepts.name: Circular buffer
concepts.statement: A circular array keeps a queue of n elements at a[j mod length(a)], a[(j+1) mod length(a)], …, a[(j+n−1) mod length(a)]: with modular arithmetic an index past length(a) − 1 wraps around to the start, so a finite array simulates an infinite one as long as the n elements fit in a.

concepts.name: ArrayQueue (array-backed FIFO queue)
concepts.statement: An ArrayQueue keeps a FIFO queue in a circular array a with j, the index of the next element to remove, and n, the number of elements: add(x) stores x in a[(j+n) mod length(a)] and remove() takes a[j] and sets j = (j+1) mod length(a), each in O(1) time ignoring resize(); resize() copies the elements into b[0], …, b[n−1] of a new array of size 2n and sets j = 0, and from an empty ArrayQueue any m operations spend O(m) time in all calls to resize().

concepts.name: Queue on a linked list with a tail pointer
concepts.statement: An SLList implements the FIFO queue operations in constant time: remove() takes the head node, as pop() does, and add(x) links a new node after tail, or makes it both head and tail when n = 0; removing from the tail instead would need the node before tail, which only n − 2 steps from head reach.

concepts.name: Stack
concepts.statement: A stack is a collection with two main operations, push (add an element) and pop (remove the most recently added one), so elements leave last in, first out; peek returns the top element without removing it. Both operations act at one end, the top. Popping or peeking an empty stack is underflow, and pushing onto a full bounded stack is overflow. An array (top counting the items) or a singly linked list (top at the head) gives O(1) push and pop, and a dynamic array amortized O(1).

concepts.name: Balanced bracket sequence
concepts.statement: A balanced bracket sequence is a string of brackets built by three rules: the empty string is balanced; if s is balanced, so is (s); if s and t are balanced, so is st. (())() is balanced, ())( is not.

concepts.name: Checking bracket balance
concepts.statement: With one bracket type, keep depth, the number of open brackets: add 1 at an opening bracket and subtract 1 at a closing one; the string is balanced when depth never goes negative and ends at 0. With several types, push every opening bracket on a stack; a closing bracket needs a non-empty stack with an opening bracket of its type on top, which it pops; the string is balanced when every check passes and the stack ends empty.

concepts.name: Minimum stack
concepts.statement: Store each stack entry as a pair: the element and the minimum of the stack from that element down. The stack’s minimum is then the top pair’s second value, and adding or removing an element stays O(1).

concepts.name: Minimum queue via a monotonic deque
concepts.statement: Keep in a deque only the elements that can still become the minimum, in nondecreasing order: before adding x, remove the trailing elements larger than x. The head is the minimum, and since each element is pushed and popped at most once, every operation is O(1) on average. Removal needs the element’s value (method 1) or its index (method 2).

concepts.name: Queue from two stacks (with minimum)
concepts.statement: Add to stack s1 and remove from stack s2, moving all of s1 into s2 (which reverses them) whenever s2 is empty. Each element is added once, transferred once and popped once, so every operation is O(1) on average; with minimum stacks, the queue’s minimum is the smaller of the two stacks’ minima.

concepts.name: Sliding window minimum
concepts.statement: The minima of all N − M + 1 subarrays of length M of an array of length N take O(N) in all: add the first M elements to a minimum queue, then repeatedly read the minimum, add the next element and remove the oldest.

concepts.name: Nearest smaller element with a stack
concepts.statement: For every position i, the nearest earlier position j with A[j] < A[i] is found in linear time by scanning with a stack: pop every top element greater than or equal to x, read the top (or none), then push x. Each pop removes an element pushed earlier, so the nested loop is linear.

concepts.name: Largest zero submatrix in O(nm)
concepts.statement: With d[j] the nearest row at or above the current row i holding a 1 in column j, each column’s best rectangle with bottom row i has top d[j] + 1, and its sides are the nearest columns left and right with a larger d, found by a stack in each direction; over all rows this is O(nm) time and O(m) memory.

concepts.name: Reverse Polish notation evaluation
concepts.statement: In reverse Polish notation the operators come after their operands. To evaluate it, read it left to right with a stack: push each number, and for an operator take the top two elements off the stack, perform the operation and put the result back. The one element left at the end is the value, found in O(n) time.

concepts.name: Infix expression parsing with two stacks
concepts.statement: With binary, left-associative operators and parentheses, an expression is evaluated in O(n) with a stack of numbers and a stack of operators kept in strictly descending priority within each pair of parentheses: push a number or an opening parenthesis; at a closing parenthesis, execute the operators back to the opening one; before pushing an operator, execute every operator on top of the same or higher priority; at the end, execute what is left. This evaluates the expression’s reverse Polish notation implicitly.

concepts.name: Unary and right-associative operators in parsing
concepts.statement: An operator is unary when it comes first, after another operator or after an opening parenthesis; it is executed on one value and given a priority above every binary operator. A right-associative operator (unary plus and minus, exponentiation) is postponed when the priorities are equal: the operators on the stack are executed only while their priority is strictly higher.

concepts.name: RootishArrayStack
concepts.statement: A RootishArrayStack stores the list in r blocks numbered 0, …, r − 1, block b holding b + 1 elements, so list index i lies in block b = i2b(i) at j = i − b(b + 1)/2; get(i) and set(i, x) take O(1) time, add(i, x) and remove(i) take O(1 + n − i), any m of them spend O(m) time in grow() and shrink(), and n elements take n + O(√n) words.

concepts.name: Square roots in constant time
concepts.statement: ⌊√x⌋ is not a word-RAM operation, but for every x ≤ n it can be computed in constant time after O(√n) preprocessing: round x down to x′, a multiple of 2^⌊r/2⌋, which lowers the root by at most 1 (√(x − a) ≥ √x − 1 for 0 ≤ a ≤ √x), look ⌊√x′⌋ up in a table sqrttab, and add 1 at most twice; a table logtab gives ⌊log x⌋, so that a small x can be shifted up first.

concepts.name: Ω(√n) wasted space is unavoidable
concepts.statement: A RootishArrayStack wastes O(√n) space, and no structure that starts empty and adds items one at a time can do better: with its items in r blocks, either r ≥ √n and the r references to the blocks are wasted, or some block holds at least n/r > √n items and was wasting √n space when it was allocated.

concepts.name: SEList (space-efficient list)
concepts.statement: An SEList with block size b is a doubly-linked list of nodes, each holding a BDeque of capacity b + 1, in which every block but the last keeps between b − 1 and b + 1 elements; locating index i takes O(1 + min{i, n − i}/b) steps, add(i, x) and remove(i) shift through at most b blocks or spread or gather b of them, and the wasted space is O(b + n/b).

concepts.name: SEList spreading and gathering
concepts.statement: Spreading b full blocks into b + 1 blocks of b, or gathering b blocks of b − 1 into b − 1 blocks of b, costs O(b²); counting fragile nodes, those whose block does not hold exactly b elements, shows that from an empty SEList any m ≥ 1 calls to add(i, x) and remove(i) spend O(bm) time in all calls to spread() and gather().

concepts.name: Deque interface
concepts.statement: A Deque is a sequence of elements with a front and a back, where elements can be added and removed at either end: addFirst(x), removeFirst(), addLast(x) and removeLast(). It generalizes both the FIFO Queue and the LIFO Queue: a Stack needs only addFirst(x) and removeFirst(), a FIFO Queue addLast(x) and removeFirst().

concepts.name: ArrayDeque
concepts.statement: An ArrayDeque keeps a list in a circular array, its element i at a[(j + i) mod length(a)], and on add(i,x) or remove(i) shifts whichever side of position i is shorter, so get(i) and set(i,x) take O(1) time and add(i,x) and remove(i) O(1 + min{i, n − i}), ignoring resize(); m calls from empty spend O(m) time in all calls to resize().

concepts.name: DualArrayDeque: a deque from two stacks
concepts.statement: A DualArrayDeque keeps a list in two ArrayStacks back to back, front holding elements 0, …, front.size() − 1 in reverse order and back the rest; balance() rebuilds them with ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉ elements whenever one holds more than three times the other. get and set take O(1) time, add(i,x) and remove(i) O(1 + min{i, n − i}) ignoring balance() and resize(), and m calls from empty spend O(m) time in all calls to balance().
